html:
An Arab historian and thinker, born in Tunis in 1332 and died in Cairo in 1406. His Muqaddimah, or Introduction, tried to explain why states rise and fall, and he is often called a forerunner of sociology and economics.

His family had come from Seville in al-Andalus. He lost both parents to the Black Death in 1348. He then spent decades serving, and plotting at, the courts of North Africa and Granada, sometimes rising to high office and sometimes landing in prison. Around 1375 he withdrew to a castle in Algeria and wrote the Muqaddimah in about six months.

His central idea is asabiyya, group feeling or solidarity. Tough peoples from the desert or mountains, bound by kinship and often by religion, conquer the soft cities. Their rulers then grow used to luxury, lose their cohesion and raise taxes, and within three or four generations a new group with stronger asabiyya replaces them. He drew his examples from what he had seen, such as the Almoravids and Almohads. He also wrote about labour as the source of value, and warned that high taxes shrink what they collect.

In 1382 he moved to Mamluk Cairo, where he taught and served as a judge under the Mamluk sultans. In 1401, when Timur besieged Damascus, Ibn Khaldun was let down the city wall in a basket to meet him, and wrote an account of their talks.

Ottoman historians later used his ideas to explain their own empire's troubles, and in the 19th and 20th centuries European scholars took him up as a founder of the study of history as a science.
